newsitem.title: USA: SoGen fund manager sees stocks as overvalued.
newsitem.headline: SoGen fund manager sees stocks as overvalued.

text.p: ORLANDO, Fla., Nov 8, Reuter - Jean-Marie Eveillard, portfolio manager of the $3.5 billion SoGen International Fund, said U.S. stocks are too rich for his blood.
"The market is very high," he told Reuters in an interview. Eveillard's fund has been given the top five-star ranking by Morningstar Inc for its "excellent" returns over the last 15 years
He said that, while some strategists insist that market and economic circumstances justify the high prices for stocks, he said, " ... I find it hard to believe that."
The U.S. market reminds him at times of the Tokyo stock market, where the bubble burst in late 1989.
Among his gauges, return on equity is too rich at nearly 20 percent for the average U.S. company, while it has usually hovered around 15 percent. Also, he said, profit margins are excessively high.

Eveillard, who was here to speak at a Charles Schwab & Co conference, also is uncomfortable with the increasing use of what he feels is creative accounting by American companies. Firms overstate the value of assets, or profits, he said.

He argued that European companies are far more conservative in their accounting. For example, they write down assets more slowly and overstate reserves for potential losses. They also keep cleaner balance sheets, he said.

As a result, Eveillard has about 22 to 23 percent of the portfolio in U.S. stocks, another 33 percent in equities in continental Europe, 6-7 percent in gold-related issues, and about 15 percent in U.S. fixed-income securities, including Brady bonds that pay about 10 percent. Another 22 percent sits in cash, up from 18 percent a year ago.
The fund holds a big stake in Brady bonds. "We see the Bradys as an equity substitute," he said.
Eveillard said that, while his gut tells him to stay clear of the U.S. and he has pared holdings down from 24 percent a year ago, he can't completely stay out.
"We're value investors," he said. "It's hard to find value today, but there are still companies that offer value."
He has found them in Europe in Investor, a Swedish holding company that has been selling at a 30 to 40 percent discount to its net asset value, and LeGrand, a French maker of low-voltage switches.
Eveillard also likes Germany and Switzerland, and noted that about half of its foreign stocks are on the continent.
Eveillard and his analysts are traditional stock pickers, who scan the globe for undervalued issues. They are loathe to make big bets, holding about 200 stocks, and 100 fixed-income securities.

While the fund is prohibited from holding more than 10 percent of voting stock in any one company, it holds about that level in non-voting stock in Allen Organ Co, which makes electronic church organs. While he likes its business, the stock has not moved as high as he wanted.

The fund's top holdings include Bank of International Settlements; Freeport McMoRan Copper and Gold preferred; Buderus AG, a German company that makes heating systems and also holds real estate assets; Hong-Kong based CDL Hotels International Ltd; and Randstad Holdings NV, a Netherlands temporary employment firm. Eveillard said the fund is in the process of selling the Randstad stake, and will buy U.S.-based Manpower.
While some might argue that Sogen is a balanced fund, Eveillard argues it is value based, using fixed income as a replacement for equities.

Year to date, the fund has gained about 11.1 percent, while the S&P 500 has risen 18.14. Morningstar said that since 1985, the fund has posted positive returns in all but one year, and has been in double digits in all but three other years.
